What Is a Futures Contract? Margin, Pricing and Examples

A futures contract is a standardised agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date, traded on an exchange. This guide works through a trade, margin, daily settlement and how futures are priced.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

How a future works: an example

Suppose a stock's futures trade at ₹1,000, with a lot of 500 shares (a simplified figure; check the exchange for current lot sizes).

ItemCalculationAmount
Contract value1,000 × 500₹5,00,000
Margin at 15%15% of 5,00,000₹75,000
Profit if price rises to ₹1,04040 × 500+₹20,000 (26.7% on margin)
Loss if price falls to ₹960−40 × 500−₹20,000 (−26.7% on margin)

A 4% move in the price becomes a 26.7% gain or loss on the margin. That is leverage, and a loss can exceed the margin you first put up.

Long and short positions

  • Long futures: you agree to buy, and you gain if the price rises.
  • Short futures: you agree to sell, and you gain if the price falls.
  • Either side can close at any time before expiry by taking the opposite position.
  • In India, stock futures are settled physically at expiry, while index futures are settled in cash.

Margin and mark to market

  • Initial margin: the deposit required to open a position, set by the exchange (usually SPAN plus exposure margin).
  • Mark to market: each day, the position is valued at the closing price, and the gain or loss is settled in cash.
  • Margin shortfall: if losses reduce your margin below the requirement, you must add money, or the broker can close your position.

How futures are priced

Fair futures price = spot price × (1 + r × t) − dividends. With spot ₹1,000, an 8% interest rate and 1 month to expiry: 1,000 × (1 + 0.08 × 1/12) = ₹1,006.67.

The gap of ₹6.67 is the cost of carry: the interest you would pay to hold the stock until expiry. If futures trade well above this price, arbitrageurs buy the stock and sell the future, which pulls the prices back together. The gap shrinks to zero by expiry.

Basis, contango and backwardation

Basis is spot price minus futures price. In contango, futures trade above spot, which is the normal state. In backwardation, futures trade below spot, which can happen with an expected dividend, heavy short selling or tight supply.

Hedging with futures

You hold shares worth ₹5,00,000 and fear a fall next month. Sell one lot of futures at ₹1,000. If the price falls to ₹900, you lose ₹50,000 on the shares and gain ₹50,000 on the futures. You have locked in the value, but you would also give up any gain if the price rises.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between futures and options?

A futures contract obliges both sides to complete the trade. An option gives the buyer a right without an obligation, for which the buyer pays a premium.

What is mark to market?

Daily revaluation of an open position at the closing price, with the gain or loss settled in cash that day.

Why does the futures price converge to the spot price at expiry?

Because at expiry, the two are the same asset for immediate delivery. Any gap would be an instant arbitrage profit.

Can you lose more than your margin in futures?

Yes. Margin is only a deposit, and your loss depends on the full contract value.
